content: Apamin is a neurotoxin that specifically inhibits SK channels, which are a subtype of calcium-activated potassium channels found in the central nervous system. This toxin is a polypeptide composed of 18 amino acids and is a component of bee venom (apitoxin). It is primarily utilized in biomedical research to investigate the electrical properties of SK channels and their involvement in the afterhyperpolarizations that occur immediately following neuronal action potentials. Apamin was originally isolated from the venom of the Western honeybee (Apis mellifera). Honeybee venom is a complex mixture containing various bioactive components, including melittin, the MCD peptide, and phospholipase A2. Chemically, apamin is a polypeptide with the amino acid sequence COOH-Cys-Asn-Cys-Lys-Ala-Pro-Glu-Thr-Ala-Leu-Cys-Ala-Arg-Arg-Cys-Gln-Gln-His-NH2. It contains two disulfide bonds, specifically between Cys1-Cys11 and Cys3-Cys15. Due to the complexity of honeybee venom, isolating apamin is challenging and typically requires techniques such as electrophoresis or chromatography. Pharmacologically, apamin binds to SK channels (small-conductance calcium-activated potassium channels) in the brain and spinal cord, inhibiting their function. It blocks the three cloned SK channel subtypes (SK1, SK2, and SK3) with varying affinities: it has the highest affinity for SK2, the lowest for SK1, and an intermediate affinity for SK3. Heteromeric SK channels exhibit intermediate sensitivity to apamin. The toxin likely acts as a pore blocker, although residues both inside and outside the pore region of SK channels contribute to apamin binding. SK channels are widely distributed in excitable and non-excitable cells, including neurons in the central nervous system, intestinal myocytes, endothelial cells, and hepatocytes. When activated, SK channels contribute to afterhyperpolarizations in neurons, which regulate neuronal excitability. Intracellular calcium binding to calmodulin activates these channels, while dissociation of calcium from calmodulin leads to channel deactivation. By inhibiting SK channels, apamin increases neuronal excitability and lowers the threshold for generating action potentials. Other toxins that block SK channels include tamapin and scyllatoxin. Symptoms of apamin poisoning or bee stings may include local effects such as burning or stinging pain, swelling, and redness. Severe systemic reactions can occur, including tongue and throat swelling, difficulty breathing, and shock. Other potential complications include optic neuritis and atrophy, atrial fibrillation, cerebral infarction, acute myocardial infarction, Fisher's syndrome, acute inflammatory polyradiculopathy (Guillain-Barré syndrome), claw hand (resulting from central effects of apamin on the spinal cord and peripheral effects causing median and ulnar neuritis with forearm flexor spasms), and dramatic hemorrhagic effects in the lungs. Patients experiencing bee venom poisoning can be treated with anti-inflammatory medications, antihistamines, and oral prednisolone. SK channels are also implicated in insulin release from pancreatic cells and play a role in memory processes, particularly in the hippocampus. These channels have been proposed as therapeutic targets for conditions such as ataxia, epilepsy, memory disorders, and potentially schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease.
